newsitem.title: POLAND: Strains show in Solidarity's election alliance.
newsitem.headline: Strains show in Solidarity's election alliance.

text.p: Tensions within the centre-right opposition alliance clustered around Poland's Solidarity trade union have burst into the open as member parties jostle for places on its lists for this year's election.

Several parties rejected proposals backed by the union to forge Solidarity Election Action (AWS) into a single party. Instead, they said they formed a coordinating committee on Sunday to reinforce the concept of the AWS as a federation.

"There are differences of opinion between those who want faster integration...and those who want to preserve their identities and retain something along the lines of a confederation," AWS spokesman Tomasz Tywonek said.
"This discussion has suddenly come into the open, due to a raising of temperatures as the election lists are drawn up," he told Reuters.

Poland's right, descended from parts of the broad democracy movement that toppled communism in 1989, was so split into tiny parties that they mostly failed to gain the minimum five percent of votes needed to enter parliament in 1993 elections.
The union has managed to bring more than 30 such factions into the AWS, currently challenging the co-ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of ex-communists for top place in opinion polls.

The AWS has a chance to form the next government if it can stay together until the polls due around September, and the union argues that a disciplined single party will be better placed to win and to govern.

But some AWS parties are anxious over the dominant role the union has reserved for itself in steering the alliance, especially because of fears that key union leaders are closest to groups representing strongly Catholic nationalist ideas.

The parties which back the idea of keeping AWS as a federation include liberal conservatives such as the 100 Movement, whose ideas are close to the political centre represented by an opposition party outside the AWS, Union for Freedom (UW).
The UW is led by Leszek Balcerowicz, who as finance minister steered Poland's market reforms after the fall of communism and who has voiced strong reservations about AWS policies.
But resistance to the notion of a single party also comes from some more right-wing formations.
AWS spokesman Tywonek said there was little danger that such arguments would break the alliance apart, as its member parties must know they have little chance on their own.
"This is just a moment of wrestling, and I don't think it is very dangerous. If anyone drops out of AWS they are condemning themselves to political oblivion," Tywonek said.

He rejected arguments from critics in AWS parties that Solidarity will have too prominent a place on election lists, saying the union will only take half of the slots at the top of such lists which attract the most votes on ballot papers.
The AWS last month produced a programme which showed that economically liberal, more centrist ideas had left their mark over sometimes populist concepts advanced by radical nationalists.
But analysts say the most crucial determinant of future AWS policies will be the balance among these factions on the AWS list and therefore in the future parliament.
